title: Names hold values
text:
A short Python bridge A variable is a name associated with a value. The equals sign assigns a value; two equals signs compare values. Quotation marks make text, while an unquoted number can take part in arithmetic. print() displays a value so you can inspect it. name = "Amira"
age = 20
next_age = age + 1
is_twenty = age == 20
print(name)
print(next_age)
print(is_twenty)
print(type(age).__name__) Describe Bilal, age 21, using name and age. Calculate his age in three years in next_age. Store the comparison of his current age with 21 in is_twenty_one, then print the results. Python names are case-sensitive: age and Age are different names.

title: A list keeps values in order
text:
A short Python bridge Square brackets create a list. Each value has a position, beginning at 0. len() counts the values, and a slice selects a range of positions. A slice includes its start position and excludes its stop position. scores = [88, 72, 91]
first_score = scores[0]
first_two = scores[0:2]
print(first_score)
print(first_two)
print(len(scores)) Select the second and third scores into result. Then add 65 to the end of scores using append(), and print the new list length. A list position is an integer. The text "0" is not the same as position 0.

title: Give a calculation a name
text:
A short Python bridge A function is a named set of instructions you can reuse. def starts a function definition, and the indented body states what it does. A parameter receives an input value when the function is called. return sends the result back so it can be saved or used in another calculation. def add_bonus(score, bonus):
    return score + bonus

first = add_bonus(72, 3)
second = add_bonus(88, 2)
print(first)
print(second) Create a function called to_percentage(points, maximum) that returns points divided by maximum, multiplied by 100. Calculate 16 out of 20 into result and print it. Indentation is part of Python syntax. Division also requires a nonzero denominator.

title: Import a tool and read an error
text:
A short Python bridge import makes a module's tools available; as gives the module a shorter name. This example uses Python's built-in math module. The try/except block catches an expected conversion error so we can read its type and message, then continue. Read the error name and the failing value before changing code. import math as m

try:
    number = float("nine")
except ValueError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__ + ": " + str(error))

number = float("9")
result = m.sqrt(number)
print("Corrected result:", result) Import math as m, set text to "25", convert text to a number, and calculate its square root in result. Print the result. Catching an error does not repair its cause. This example prints the expected error and then supplies a valid value explicitly.

title: What are the key and the value?
text:
Start with a dictionary A dictionary stores pairs: a key and its value. The key is a name you use to find a value, such as "Name" or "Age". Curly brackets create the dictionary; a colon separates each key from its value. Here, one dictionary describes one fictional student. # Text uses quotes. A whole number does not need quotes.
student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
print(student)
print(type(student).__name__)
print(len(student)) Create a dictionary for Bilal, age 21, at Dubai. Add a fourth key called Program with value IT. Print the dictionary and its number of pairs. Do not mix up braces { } for dictionaries with brackets [ ] used for lists and access.

title: Find a value by its key
text:
Start with a dictionary Square brackets after a dictionary look up a key. The key must match exactly, including upper and lower case. get() is useful when a key might be missing: you can supply a default value instead of raising KeyError. student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
print(student["Name"])
print(student["Age"])
print(student.get("Email", "Not provided")) Store the campus in campus. Use get() to request Program with the default "Undeclared" and save the value in program. Store whether "Age" is a key in has_age. Print all three values. A default from get() does not insert the missing key into the dictionary.

title: Change, add, and remove a pair
text:
Start with a dictionary Assigning a value to an existing key replaces its old value. Assigning to a new key adds a pair. pop() removes a key and returns its value. A dictionary cannot hold two separate entries with the same key. student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
student["Age"] = 21
student["Program"] = "AI"
removed = student.pop("Campus")
print(student)
print("Removed:", removed) Start with the same original dictionary. Increase Age by 2, add Program as IT, and remove Campus. Print the final dictionary. pop() raises KeyError for an absent key unless you also provide a default.

title: Read all keys and all pairs
A list has positions
text:
From one student to many A list stores values in order. Positions start at 0, so names[1] is the second value. A slice such as [0:2] includes positions 0 and 1 but excludes position 2. A negative position counts back from the end. names = ["Amira", "Bilal", "Chloe", "Dana"]
print(names[0])
print(names[-1])
result = names[0:2]
print(result) Select only Bilal and Chloe into result using one slice. Then append Ethan and print the new list length. A single position returns one item; a slice returns a list, even if it contains one item.

title: A dictionary of lists describes columns
text:
From one student to many Now each dictionary value is a list. The keys describe future column names, and values at the same position belong to the same student. data["Age"] chooses a list; the second pair of brackets chooses an item inside that list. data = {
    "Name": ["Amira", "Bilal", "Chloe"],
    "Age": [20, 21, 19],
    "Campus": ["RAK", "Dubai", "RAK"]
}
print(data["Name"])
print(data["Age"][1])
print(data["Name"][1], data["Campus"][1]) Change Chloe's age from 19 to 20 without changing the other ages. Print Chloe's name and updated age. Positions in lists are numbers; dictionary keys can be text. Do not swap their roles.

title: A list of dictionaries describes rows
text:
From one student to many A second arrangement stores one dictionary per student inside a list. Each dictionary is a record, or row. rows[1] selects the second record; ["Name"] then selects a field within it. Both arrangements can later become a pandas DataFrame. rows = [
    {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"},
    {"Name": "Bilal", "Age": 21, "Campus": "Dubai"},
    {"Name": "Chloe", "Age": 19, "Campus": "RAK"}
]
print(rows[1])
print(rows[1]["Name"])
print(len(rows)) Add Dana, age 22, at Dubai as a fourth dictionary. Print the last student's name and the total record count. Count records with len(rows); len(rows[0]) counts fields in the first record.

title: Check lengths before making a table
One column, with labels
text:
Meet the pandas Series The setup imports pandas using the short name pd. A Series is a one-dimensional collection of values with an index: labels attached to those values. Without an explicit index, pandas supplies labels starting at 0. A Series also has a dtype describing how its values are stored. scores = pd.Series([88, 72, 91], name="Score")
print(scores)
print("Number of values:", len(scores))
print("Index:", scores.index.tolist()) Create a Series called hours containing 8, 5, and 9. Give it the name Study_Hours and print its length. Do not call the dtype text a data row; it describes the Series.

title: Choose labels or positions explicitly
text:
Meet the pandas Series You can supply meaningful labels, such as student IDs, as the Series index. loc selects an index label; iloc selects an integer position. These can identify the same value, but they ask different questions. Using them explicitly avoids confusing a number used as a label with a position. scores = pd.Series([88, 72, 91], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], name="Score")
by_label = scores.loc["S002"]
by_position = scores.iloc[1]
print(scores)
print(by_label, by_position) Select S003 by label and the first score by position. Store them as by_label and by_position, then print both. Prefer .iloc[0] when you mean first position; do not rely on scores[0] with a text index.

title: Do arithmetic on a whole Series
text:
Meet the pandas Series Pandas can apply an arithmetic operation to all values at once. This is called a vectorized operation. scores + 2 creates a new result; it does not replace scores unless you assign the result back. clip() can enforce an upper or lower boundary when that is the stated rule. scores = pd.Series([88, 72, 99], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], name="Score")
result = scores + 2
print("Original:")
print(scores)
print("After adding two:")
print(result) Add 5 to each score, then cap the result at 100. Keep the original scores unchanged. Use clipping only when a justified business or teaching rule calls for it.

title: Labels control Series alignment
text:
Meet the pandas Series When combining two Series, pandas matches index labels, even when their order differs. It does not simply pair the first value in one Series with the first value in the other. A label missing from one side normally produces a missing result for arithmetic. quiz = pd.Series({"S001": 17, "S002": 14, "S003": 19})
project = pd.Series({"S003": 46, "S001": 44, "S002": 36})
result = quiz + project
print(result) Remove S002 from project, add the two Series again, and print which result is missing. Do not replace the missing project with zero. Equal lengths do not guarantee correct alignment; inspect the actual index labels.

title: Make a table from a dictionary
text:
Build and inspect a DataFrame A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table with rows and named columns. Pass a dictionary of equally long lists to pd.DataFrame(). Each dictionary key becomes a column name. Each list position supplies the values for one row. data = {"Name": ["Amira", "Bilal", "Chloe"], "Age": [20, 21, 19]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)
print(type(df).__name__)
print("Rows and columns:", df.shape) Add a Campus list with RAK, Dubai, and RAK to data before building df. Print the new table and shape. Call pd.DataFrame(...) with a capital D and F; Python names are case-sensitive.

title: Build a table from records
text:
Build and inspect a DataFrame A list of dictionaries can also become a DataFrame. Each dictionary contributes a row, and pandas matches fields by their keys. If one record lacks a field, pandas marks that cell as missing. The table therefore does not require every record to contain the same keys. rows = [
    {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"},
    {"Name": "Bilal", "Age": 21},
    {"Name": "Chloe", "Age": 19, "Campus": "RAK"}
]
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df)
print("Missing campus:", df["Campus"].isna().sum()) Add Campus as Dubai to Bilal's record before constructing df. Check that no campus values are missing. Missing-value display can vary with dtype and pandas version; inspect it with isna().

title: Look at the beginning and the end
text:
Build and inspect a DataFrame The setup provides students(), a helper that returns a fresh copy of the 12-row fictional practice table. head(n) shows the first n rows and tail(n) shows the last n rows. These previews help you understand a file without printing the whole dataset. A preview alone does not prove every row is valid. df = students()
first = df.head(3)
last = df.tail(2)
print("First three rows:")
print(first)
print("Last two rows:")
print(last) Show the first two rows and last three rows. Print the full table's shape to confirm previews have not removed rows. head() without an argument defaults to five rows, or fewer when fewer exist.

title: Inspect names, types, and a first summary
text:
Build and inspect a DataFrame Attributes such as shape and columns are stored information, so they do not use parentheses. Methods such as info() perform an action and do use parentheses. info() reports column names, non-missing counts, and dtypes; describe() returns summary statistics. Text dtype labels can differ across pandas versions, so focus on what the data represent. df = students()
print("Columns:", df.columns.tolist())
print("Shape:", df.shape)
df.info()
summary = df[["Age", "Score"]].describe()
print(summary.round(2)) Inspect dtypes, then create a describe() summary for Study_Hours and Attendance only. Round it to one decimal place. Call df.info() directly. print(df.info()) also prints None because info() returns None.

title: One bracket or two?
text:
Select exactly what you need df["Score"] selects one column as a Series. df[["Score"]] passes a list of column names and returns a DataFrame, even with only one column. To select several columns, put their names in that inner list. The distinction matters when another operation expects a table. df = students()
column = df["Score"]
table = df[["Score"]]
result = df[["Name", "Score"]]
print(type(column).__name__, column.shape)
print(type(table).__name__, table.shape)
print(result.head(3)) Select Campus and Program, in that order, into a DataFrame named result. Print its first four rows and shape. df["Name", "Score"] is not the same as df[["Name", "Score"]] for these ordinary columns.

title: Select row and column labels with loc
text:
Select exactly what you need set_index("Student_ID") uses the student IDs as row labels and, by default, removes that field from the data columns. loc has the form table.loc[row_labels, column_labels]. A list keeps the selection table-shaped. at is convenient when you need a single value with a row label and column label. df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
result = df.loc[["S001", "S003"], ["Name", "Score"]]
one_score = df.at["S003", "Score"]
print(result)
print("One score:", one_score) Select S002 and S004 with Name and Campus into result. Use at to get S004's Score into one_score. set_index does not automatically check that IDs are unique; uniqueness needs its own check.

title: Select row and column positions with iloc
text:
Select exactly what you need iloc uses numerical positions for both rows and columns. Positions start at 0 even when the printed index labels are student IDs. A slice excludes its stop position. iat reads one value using a row position and a column position. df = students()[["Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
result = df.iloc[1:4, [0, 2]]
one_score = df.iat[1, 2]
print(result)
print("One score:", one_score) Select the first two rows and all three columns into result. Read the first student's score with iat into one_score. iloc expects positions, so df.iloc["S001"] is not valid positional selection.

title: Compare the two slice endpoints
text:
Select exactly what you need For this sorted, unique index, a loc label slice includes both its start and stop labels. An iloc position slice excludes its stop position. Compare the selected IDs instead of assuming the two expressions return the same rows. Label slicing works best when the index is appropriately sorted and its labels are understood. df = students().set_index("Student_ID").sort_index()
by_label = df.loc["S002":"S004", ["Name", "Score"]]
by_position = df.iloc[1:3][["Name", "Score"]]
print("Label slice:")
print(by_label)
print("Position slice:")
print(by_position) Change by_position so that its position slice returns exactly the same three rows as by_label. Store the Boolean equality check in same, then print the selected rows and the check. Selecting from a selection is fine for reading; use one .loc assignment when changing the original table.

title: See the True and False values first
text:
Filter with conditions Comparing a Series with a value produces a Boolean Series, often called a mask. Each True marks a row that meets the condition. df.loc[mask, columns] keeps those rows and selects the requested columns. Keeping the mask in its own variable makes the logic easier to inspect. df = students()
mask = df["Score"] > 80
print(mask)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result) Change the condition to Score < 70. Select Student_ID, Name, and Score into result. Print the number of matches. A mask should correspond to the table being filtered; a mask from another table can misalign.

title: Combine conditions with AND and OR
text:
Filter with conditions Use & for element-by-element AND and | for element-by-element OR. Put parentheses around each comparison before combining them. AND requires both conditions; OR requires at least one. Python's and and or do not combine pandas Series masks this way. df = students()
mask = (df["Campus"] == "RAK") & (df["Score"] >= 80)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
print(result) Select students who are at RAK OR have Score at least 90. Keep the same four output columns. Do not omit the parentheses around comparisons; operator precedence can change the expression.

title: Membership, ranges, and NOT
text:
Filter with conditions isin() tests whether a value belongs to an allowed list. between() checks a range; inclusive="both" includes its two endpoints. The ~ operator reverses a Boolean mask. Naming masks can make a longer rule easier to explain. df = students()
in_program = df["Program"].isin(["AI"])
in_range = df["Score"].between(70, 90, inclusive="both")
result = df.loc[in_program & in_range, ["Name", "Program", "Score"]]
print(result) Select students whose Program is NOT AI and whose Score is between 70 and 85 inclusive. Print their names, programs, and scores. Do not use Program == ["AI", "IT"] to test membership; use .isin(["AI", "IT"]).

title: Read a filter written with query
text:
Filter with conditions query() is another way to express a row filter, using a short expression in a string. Column names appear inside that expression. @limit refers to a Python variable outside it. Learn the normal Boolean-mask form first so you can check what the query means. df = students()
limit = 85
result = df.query("Score >= @limit and Campus == 'Dubai'")[["Name", "Campus", "Score"]]
print(result) Use a normal Boolean mask instead of query to find Dubai students with Score at least 80. Save the same three columns in result. Use fixed, trusted query expressions for these lessons; do not construct executable expressions from arbitrary user text.

title: Sort rows by a value
text:
Sorting and index decisions sort_values() orders whole rows by one or more column values. ascending=False puts larger values first. It returns a new table, so assign the result if you want to keep the order. The index labels travel with their rows and are not automatically renumbered. df = students()
result = df.sort_values("Score", ascending=False).head(3)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]])
print("Index labels:", result.index.tolist()) Find the three lowest scores instead. Keep Student_ID, Name, and Score in result. head(3) before sorting chooses the first three source rows, not the three highest scores.

title: Specify a tie rule
Set, check, and reset an index
text:
Sorting and index decisions An index labels rows; it is not automatically a unique ID. set_index() chooses the labels, and index.is_unique tells you whether any label repeats. reset_index() moves the current index back into a column and supplies new default row labels. Use reset_index(drop=True) only when you deliberately want to discard the current labels. df = students()
indexed = df.set_index("Student_ID")
print("Unique index:", indexed.index.is_unique)
result = indexed.reset_index()
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name"]].head(3)) Set Student_ID as the index, select S003 and S001 in that order, and reset the selected index without losing the IDs. Having an index does not guarantee that its labels are unique or non-missing.

title: Reindex to a requested order
text:
Sorting and index decisions reindex() aligns a table to a specified set of labels and their requested order. Existing labels bring their rows with them; new labels create missing values. This differs from sorting because you supply the desired labels explicitly. Use isna() to inspect newly missing cells. df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
result = df.reindex(["S003", "S001", "S999"])[["Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
print("Missing name:")
print(result["Name"].isna()) Reindex to S002, S001, and S004, in that order. Confirm that none of their names is missing. Reindexing can fail when source labels are duplicated; check uniqueness before using labels as identifiers.

title: Calculate a new column
text:
Create and update columns Assign a Series to a new column name to add a field. Arithmetic across columns works row by row after index alignment. Here the artificial Score_Per_Hour ratio demonstrates division; it is not a validated measure of student ability. Always consider units and the meaning of a calculation. df = students()
df["Score_Per_Hour"] = df["Score"] / df["Study_Hours"]
result = df[["Name", "Score", "Study_Hours", "Score_Per_Hour"]]
print(result.head(3).round(2)) Start with a fresh df = students(). Create Score_Fraction by dividing Score by 100. Store Name, Score, and Score_Fraction for all students in result, then print its first three rows. Before dividing by a column, check for zero and missing denominators; they can create undefined results.

title: Use assign, rename, and drop
text:
Create and update columns assign() returns a DataFrame with new or replaced columns. rename(columns=...) changes column labels, while drop(columns=...) removes named columns. These methods return new objects by default. Assign the returned result so your intended changes are kept. df = students()
result = (df.assign(Passed=df["Score"] >= 60)
            .rename(columns={"Name": "Student_Name"})
            .drop(columns=["Join_Date"]))
print(result[["Student_Name", "Score", "Passed"]].head(4))
print("Result shape:", result.shape) Use assign to create Needs_Support for scores below 70. Rename Attendance to Attendance_Percent and drop Join_Date. Keep the result in result. Calling df.drop(...) without assigning its returned result does not change df by default.

title: Update the original with one loc assignment
text:
Create and update columns Use one .loc[row_condition, column_name] assignment to change selected values in a DataFrame. This explicitly identifies both the rows and the field being changed. Avoid chained assignment such as df[mask]["Score"] = value; it does not reliably update the intended original object and does not do so under pandas 3 Copy-on-Write. df = students()
mask = df["Student_ID"] == "S004"
df.loc[mask, "Score"] = 67
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result) Apply a practice bonus of 3 points to students with Attendance at least 95. Cap scores at 100 and show only the updated students. Repeatedly running an incremental update on the same table would repeat the bonus; this cell starts with a fresh table each time.

title: Keep an independent working copy
text:
Create and update columns Assigning original to another name creates an alias: both names refer to the same Python object. copy() creates a separate DataFrame for this ordinary scalar-valued teaching table. Use a fresh copy when you want to experiment without changing the original. Pandas copy rules do not replace the need to understand which object you are editing. original = students()
working = original.copy()
working.loc[0, "Score"] = 0
print("Original first score:", original.loc[0, "Score"])
print("Working first score:", working.loc[0, "Score"])
print("Same object:", working is original) Copy only the RAK rows into working. Add 1 to their scores in the copy and verify Amira's original score is still 88. For columns containing nested mutable Python objects, even a deep DataFrame copy does not recursively copy those inner objects; this table uses ordinary scalar values.

title: A number and its text are different
text:
Data types and safe conversion A data type tells pandas what a column contains and which operations make sense. Quotation marks make "20" text. `astype()` converts values when the requested conversion is possible. ages = pd.Series(["20", "21", "19"], dtype="string")
result = ages.astype("int64")
print("Before:", ages.dtype)
print("After:", result.dtype)
print("Next year:", (result + 1).tolist()) Start again with the same text ages. Convert them to numbers and calculate their mean in `result`. Do not assume a column is numeric just because its displayed values look like numbers.

title: Convert messy numbers and keep the reason
text:
Data types and safe conversion `pd.to_numeric()` parses values as numbers. With `errors="coerce"`, values it cannot parse become missing. Preserve the source so you can distinguish an invalid label from a value that was already missing. source = pd.Series(["88", "absent", None, "72"], dtype="string")
numbers = pd.to_numeric(source, errors="coerce")
invalid = source.notna() & numbers.isna()
result = pd.DataFrame({"Original": source, "Number": numbers, "Invalid_text": invalid})
print(result) Change "absent" to "90" in the source. Rebuild the table and count the missing numbers. Do not silently turn every conversion failure into zero.

title: Integers that can be missing
text:
Data types and safe conversion Pandas nullable integer type `Int64` can store whole numbers and `pd.NA`. Its capital I matters. Comparisons can also be missing, so decide how missing comparisons should behave in a filter. ages = pd.Series([20, None, 22], dtype="Int64")
result = ages + 1
print(result)
print("Known ages:", ages.notna().sum()) Start with the same ages and keep only known ages of at least 21. Store the filtered Series in `result`. Do not write `if pd.NA:`; its truth value is ambiguous. Use `.isna()` or `.notna()`.

title: Categories and an explicit order
text:
Data types and safe conversion A category stores values drawn from a defined set, such as programs or rating bands. An ordered category has a meaningful sequence that you choose. Sorting follows that sequence instead of alphabetical order. ratings = pd.Series(["High", "Low", "Medium", "Low"], dtype="string")
rating_type = pd.CategoricalDtype(["Low", "Medium", "High"], ordered=True)
result = ratings.astype(rating_type).sort_values()
print(result)
print("Order:", result.cat.categories.tolist()) Use students(). Make Program an ordered category with IT before AI, then sort by Program and Student_ID. Store the sorted Student_ID and Program columns in the DataFrame result. A value outside a declared category list becomes missing when converted; check the result.

title: Missing is not the same as empty or zero
text:
Missing values and honest cleaning `isna()` gives True where a value is missing. Zero is a recorded value, and an empty string is text unless you explicitly treat it as missing. Counting True values with `.sum()` counts missing entries. values = pd.Series([0, None, "", pd.NA, np.nan], dtype="object")
result = values.isna()
print(result.tolist())
print("Missing count:", result.sum()) Treat the empty string as missing, but keep zero. Store the cleaned Series in `result` and count missing entries. Use `.isna()`, not `== np.nan`, to detect missing values.

title: Drop rows only for required fields
text:
Missing values and honest cleaning `dropna(subset=[...])` removes rows missing the specified fields. It does not remove a row just because an unrelated field is missing. Keep a count of excluded records and consider how the exclusion affects the answer. df = raw_students()
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce")
result = df.dropna(subset=["Score"])
print(result[["Student_ID", "Score", "Study_Hours"]])
print("Rows kept:", len(result)) Keep only rows with both Score and Study_Hours available. Leave the intentional duplicate for the next module. Removing incomplete records can change the composition of your data; report what was excluded.

title: Fill a label without inventing a measurement
text:
Missing values and honest cleaning `fillna()` replaces missing values with a value you specify. A label such as "Unknown" can make a missing category visible in a report. The same idea does not justify inventing a score or age. campuses = pd.Series(["RAK", None, "Dubai", None], dtype="string")
result = campuses.fillna("Unknown")
print(result.tolist()) Use the same Series, but first record a Boolean Was_missing flag. Store a DataFrame named result with the filled Campus column and the Was_missing flag. Do not use zero as a universal replacement for missing numbers.

title: Compare a fill policy with keeping missing data
text:
Missing values and honest cleaning Preview of Module 16: the groupby, transform, and named aggregation syntax in this cell will be explained there. First focus on the difference between a technical replacement and a justified data policy. A group median is one possible imputation rule, not a universal answer. `transform()` returns a group result for every original row. This small example compares a proposed fill with the original values so its effect is visible. df = pd.DataFrame({"Program": ["AI", "AI", "AI", "IT", "IT"], "Hours": [4.0, 8.0, np.nan, 2.0, np.nan]})
group_median = df.groupby("Program")["Hours"].transform("median")
result = df.assign(Hours_filled=df["Hours"].fillna(group_median), Was_missing=df["Hours"].isna())
print(result) Use the same original table. Keep the missing values and store a summary in result with Program as its index. Name the known Hours count Known_hours, the row count Rows, and the median Median_hours. In predictive modeling, fit any imputation rule on training data only; do not learn it from held-out test data.

title: Find an exact repeated record
text:
Duplicates and data quality `duplicated()` marks repeated rows. By default, the first occurrence is kept unmarked and later copies are marked True. With `keep=False`, every member of a repeated set is marked. df = raw_students()
result = df.loc[df.duplicated(keep=False), ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
print("Extra copies:", df.duplicated().sum()) Remove exact duplicate rows and reset the index. Store the result in `result`. A duplicate record and a missing value are different problems.

title: A repeated ID is not always an exact duplicate
text:
Duplicates and data quality `subset` lets you check only the columns that define a record key. Two rows can share an ID but disagree on a score. Keeping the last one is defensible only when a documented order says it is the latest record. df = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": ["S001", "S001", "S002"], "Updated": ["2026-10-01", "2026-10-03", "2026-10-02"], "Score": [80, 88, 72]})
result = df.loc[df.duplicated(subset=["Student_ID"], keep=False)]
print(result)
print("Exact duplicates:", df.duplicated().sum()) Assume the later Updated date is the authoritative revision. Parse Updated, sort chronologically, and keep the latest row per Student_ID. Store the retained rows in result, sorted by Student_ID in ascending order. In a transaction table, repeated student IDs may be expected; define what one row represents.

title: Flag impossible values instead of hiding them
text:
Duplicates and data quality Data can have the right type and still be invalid. If Attendance is a percentage, its allowed range is 0 through 100. A Boolean mask can create a review table before you decide how to repair the source. df = raw_students()
invalid = ~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100)
result = df.loc[invalid, ["Student_ID", "Attendance"]]
print(result) Preserve the source Attendance values in Attendance_raw. Convert Attendance to a nullable numeric column and set its out-of-range values to missing. Store the affected rows in result with columns Student_ID, Attendance_raw, and Attendance. The allowed range comes from the meaning of the variable, not from pandas.

title: Turn expectations into assertions
text:
Duplicates and data quality An assertion stops execution if an expectation is false. It is useful for classroom checks and analysis pipelines. Validate identity, required values, and ranges separately so a failure has a clear meaning. df = students()
assert df["Student_ID"].notna().all(), "A student ID is missing"
assert df["Student_ID"].is_unique, "Student IDs must be unique here"
assert df["Score"].between(0, 100).all(), "Score outside 0-100"
result = {"rows": len(df), "valid_ids": True, "valid_scores": True}
print(result) Add checks requiring Campus to be RAK or Dubai and Attendance to be 0-100. Store the two Boolean results in a dictionary named result with keys campus_ok and attendance_ok. Python can disable assert statements in optimized runs; formal applications may need explicit validation errors.

title: Clean spaces and preserve meaningful labels
text:
Clean and search text The `.str` accessor applies text operations to each entry in a Series. `strip()` removes spaces at the beginning and end. A label map can then standardize spelling while preserving the exact labels you want. df = raw_students()
df["Name"] = df["Name"].astype("string").str.strip()
result = df.loc[df["Student_ID"] == "S001", ["Student_ID", "Name"]]
print(result) Standardize all Campus labels as exactly RAK or Dubai. Handle case and surrounding spaces before mapping. Store Student_ID and the cleaned Campus for every source row in result. An unrecognized value passed through a dictionary map becomes missing; inspect unmatched labels.

title: Literal text and regular expressions
text:
Clean and search text `str.contains()` checks whether text contains a pattern. Use `regex=False` when you want the characters literally. With a regular expression, characters such as a dot can have special meanings. files = pd.Series(["report.csv", "reportXcsv", "notes.csv", None, "csv.backup"], dtype="string")
mask = files.str.contains(".csv", regex=False, na=False)
result = files[mask]
print(result) Select all nonmissing filenames that begin with report. Use a regular expression and store the result. Always be clear whether a pattern is literal text or a regular expression.

title: Split a value into separate columns
text:
Clean and search text `str.split()` separates text at a delimiter. `expand=True` creates separate columns rather than a list in each cell. Limiting splits can protect the rest of a string when a delimiter appears repeatedly. emails = pd.Series(["amira@example.edu", "bilal@example.edu", None], dtype="string")
result = emails.str.split("@", n=1, expand=True, regex=False)
result.columns = ["Username", "Domain"]
print(result) Use the same emails. Extract Domain as a Series, then store the frequency of each known domain in result as a value_counts() Series. This is a string-processing exercise, not full validation of every legal email address.

title: Extract only values that match a structure
text:
Clean and search text `str.extract()` uses capture groups to pull parts out of a matching pattern. Named groups become useful column names. A nonmatching string produces missing fields, which you should inspect. codes = pd.Series(["AI-101", "IT-205", None, "bad"], dtype="string")
result = codes.str.extract(r"^(?P<Program>[A-Z]+)-(?P<Number>\d+)$")
print(result) Use the same codes. Extract the fields and convert Number to nullable Int64. A successful pattern match checks structure, not whether the code exists in an official registry.

title: Turn date text into dates
text:
Dates, times, and durations A date-looking string is still text until it is parsed. `to_datetime()` converts it to a date/time type. An explicit format removes ambiguity; impossible dates can be marked as NaT, pandas missing date value. source = pd.Series(["2026-09-01", "2026-09-03", "2026-02-30"], dtype="string")
result = pd.to_datetime(source, format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
print(result)
print("Unparsed dates:", result.isna().sum()) Parse ["01/09/2026", "03/09/2026", "30/02/2026"] as day/month/year. Count invalid dates. Inspect parsing failures; errors="coerce" does not repair the source date.

title: Extract useful calendar parts
text:
Dates, times, and durations After parsing dates, the `.dt` accessor exposes calendar parts such as year, month, and weekday. These features are useful for grouping and checking patterns. Do not try to use `.dt` on unparsed strings. df = students()
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df[["Student_ID", "Join_Date"]].copy()
result["Month"] = result["Join_Date"].dt.month
result["Weekday"] = result["Join_Date"].dt.day_name()
print(result.head(4)) Add Year and Day columns for the same join dates. Store only the first three rows in result, with columns Student_ID, Year, Month, and Day, then print result. A weekday pattern in twelve fictional records is a practice result, not evidence about real student behavior.

title: Filter an explicit date interval
text:
Dates, times, and durations Date comparisons let you select a time interval. `between()` includes both boundaries by default; naming the inclusive rule makes your intent clearer. Here every date is a midnight date with no separate time-of-day information. df = students()
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
mask = df["Join_Date"].between("2026-09-03", "2026-09-06", inclusive="both")
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Join_Date"]]
print(result) Select dates on or after September 3 and strictly before September 6 using two comparisons. With timestamps containing hours, an end date at midnight is not the whole final day; a next-day exclusive bound is often clearer.

title: Calculate elapsed time with a fixed reference
text:
Dates, times, and durations Subtracting dates produces timedeltas, which represent durations. `.dt.days` extracts whole days from those durations. A fixed reference date makes a classroom result reproducible when the file is opened later. df = students()
joined = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
reference = pd.Timestamp("2026-10-01")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": df["Student_ID"], "Days_enrolled": (reference - joined).dt.days})
print(result.head(4)) Change the reference to October 8 and select students with at least 30 elapsed days enrolled. For real timestamps, keep time zones consistent before subtracting them.

title: Map codes to meaningful labels
text:
Map, apply, and vectorize `Series.map()` can look up each value in a dictionary. A code missing from the dictionary produces a missing result. Keep the source codes so you can investigate labels that were not mapped. codes = pd.Series(["AI", "IT", "CS", None], dtype="string")
labels = {"AI": "Artificial Intelligence", "IT": "Information Technology"}
result = pd.DataFrame({"Code": codes, "Label": codes.map(labels)})
print(result) For this exercise, define CS as Cybersecurity. Add it to the mapping and rebuild the result while leaving the original missing code missing. The meaning of a code must come from a stated codebook, not a guess.

title: Apply a function to each value
text:
Map, apply, and vectorize A Python function can express a custom rule for one value. `Series.apply()` calls that function for each entry. When the same rule can be written with built-in column operations, those operations are often simpler and more efficient. scores = pd.Series([58, 79, 80, 95])
def status(score):
    return "Secure" if score >= 80 else "Review"
result = scores.apply(status)
print(result.tolist()) Create the same labels without a custom function. Use a Boolean comparison and a mapping from True/False to labels. These labels use an exercise rule, not an official grading policy.

title: A row function versus column arithmetic
text:
Map, apply, and vectorize `DataFrame.apply(..., axis=1)` passes one row at a time to a function. Here Quiz is out of 20 and Project is out of 50, so both must be scaled before weighting them. A direct column formula can express the same calculation. df = pd.DataFrame({"Quiz": [16, 12, 18], "Project": [40, 35, 45]})
result = df.apply(lambda row: (row["Quiz"] / 20) * 40 + (row["Project"] / 50) * 60, axis=1)
print(result.round(2).tolist()) Compute the same weighted percentage with direct column arithmetic, without apply or lambda. Check the maximum points and weights before calculating a percentage.

title: Fixed intervals versus quantile groups
text:
Map, apply, and vectorize `cut()` groups numbers using value boundaries that you choose. `qcut()` uses sample quantiles to form groups with roughly similar counts. They answer different questions, and equal-count groups need not have equal numeric widths. values = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 100])
fixed = pd.cut(values, bins=[0, 50, 100], labels=["Lower", "Upper"], include_lowest=True)
quantile = pd.qcut(values, q=2, labels=["Lower_half", "Upper_half"])
result = pd.DataFrame({"Value": values, "Fixed_band": fixed, "Quantile_band": quantile})
print(result) Use students(). Create Score_band using boundaries 0, 60, 80, 100 with labels Developing, Progressing, Secure. Include both 0 and 100, with 60 in Developing and 80 in Progressing. Store the count of each band in a Series named result. Tied values can prevent qcut from making the requested number of distinct bins; inspect boundaries and group counts.

title: Mean and median respond differently
text:
Statistics you can explain The mean uses every numeric value in an arithmetic average. The median is the middle value after sorting. Comparing them can help you notice how an unusually large or small observation affects a summary. costs = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])  # Fictional costs in AED
result = pd.Series({"Mean_AED": costs.mean(), "Median_AED": costs.median()})
print(result) Change the last cost from 50 to 500. Recalculate mean and median in result. An extreme value is not automatically a mistake; investigate its source and meaning.

title: Spread and the standard-deviation convention
text:
Statistics you can explain Standard deviation measures spread around the mean in the same units as the values. pandas uses sample standard deviation by default, with ddof=1. ddof=0 uses the population-style denominator; choose based on what the data represent. hours = pd.Series([2.0, 4.0, 6.0])
result = pd.Series({"Mean_hours": hours.mean(), "Sample_std_hours": hours.std(ddof=1), "Population_std_hours": hours.std(ddof=0)})
print(result.round(4)) Replace the hours with [4.0, 4.0, 4.0]. Recalculate both standard deviations. With only one known value, sample std is missing because n - 1 is zero.

title: Describe, count, and quantiles
text:
Statistics you can explain `describe()` summarizes a numeric Series with count, mean, spread, and selected percentiles. Count excludes missing values; size counts all entries. A quantile describes a position in the distribution, and its value may be interpolated between observations. scores = pd.Series([60.0, 70.0, np.nan, 80.0, 90.0])
result = scores.describe()
print(result)
print("Rows:", scores.size, "Known:", scores.count()) For the same scores, report the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles explicitly using quantile. Describe is a starting point. It does not check whether IDs, units, ranges, or collection procedures are valid.

title: Correlation describes association
text:
Statistics you can explain `corr()` computes pairwise correlations between numeric variables; its default method is Pearson correlation. Positive values indicate that higher values tend to occur together in a linear pattern. Correlation does not establish that one variable causes the other. df = students()
result = df[["Study_Hours", "Score", "Attendance"]].corr(method="pearson")
print(result.round(3)) Calculate Spearman rank correlation for Study_Hours and Score. Store the two-by-two matrix in result. Missing entries are handled pairwise, so different correlations can use different numbers of observations.

title: One question for each group
text:
Group, summarize, and compare `groupby()` splits rows according to a label, then a summary method calculates one result per group. Named aggregation lets you choose readable output names. Here each campus receives its own row count and mean score. df = students()
result = df.groupby("Campus", as_index=False).agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"), Mean_score=("Score", "mean"))
print(result.round(2)) Group by Program instead. Store a DataFrame named result with Program as a normal column and named summary columns Students, Median_score, and Highest_score. A mean without its supporting count can hide a very small group.

title: Multiple keys and missing group labels
text:
Group, summarize, and compare Grouping by a list of columns forms one group for each observed combination. By default, rows with a missing group key are excluded. `dropna=False` keeps those rows in a separate missing-label group so the totals can be audited. df = students()
df.loc[0, "Campus"] = None
result = df.groupby(["Campus", "Program"], dropna=False, as_index=False).agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"), Mean_score=("Score", "mean"))
print(result.round(2))
print("Total represented:", result["Students"].sum()) Run the same grouping with dropna=True. Compare its represented row total with len(df), and store the grouped table in result. When group keys are categorical, set observed explicitly if you need predictable inclusion of unused categories.

title: A summary for every original row
text:
Group, summarize, and compare `transform()` returns values aligned with the original rows. A group mean can therefore be attached to every student in that group. This makes comparisons with a group benchmark possible without reducing the table to one row per group. df = students()
df["Program_mean"] = df.groupby("Program")["Score"].transform("mean")
df["Difference"] = df["Score"] - df["Program_mean"]
result = df[["Student_ID", "Program", "Score", "Program_mean", "Difference"]]
print(result.round(2)) Calculate the median score within each campus in a column named Campus_median. Keep only students scoring strictly above that median. Store Student_ID, Campus, Score, and Campus_median in result. A group-relative label and a fixed-threshold label answer different questions.

title: Keep whole groups and control unused categories
text:
Group, summarize, and compare A group filter keeps or removes whole groups based on a group-level rule. Categorical columns can also contain labels with no rows. `observed=True` limits a group result to categories actually present in the data. df = students()
df["Program"] = pd.Categorical(df["Program"], categories=["AI", "IT", "CS"])
result = df.groupby("Program", observed=True)["Score"].agg(["size", "mean"])
print(result.round(2)) Start from students(). Keep all students in programs whose mean Score is at least 80 using groupby().filter(). Unused categories and missing labels are different: observed controls unused categories; dropna controls missing keys.

title: Attach the department
text:
Merge related tables The Program column is a key shared by two tables. A many-to-one merge lets several students match one department row. The validation checks that the lookup table has only one row per program. df = students()
result = df.merge(departments(), on="Program", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
print(result[["Student_ID", "Program", "Department"]]) Use DataFrame.join to attach the same lookup fields. Set Program as the lookup index and keep the student index. Do not join tables by row position when they describe entities identified by keys.

title: Keep matches or keep every student
text:
Merge related tables An inner merge keeps only keys found in both tables. A left merge keeps every key from the left table. In this complete assessment lookup, a missing Quiz comes from an unmatched student. With other data, a matched assessment could itself have a missing Quiz; use the merge indicator to test for unmatched records. result = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="inner", validate="one_to_one")
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name", "Quiz"]])
print("Rows:", len(result)) Change the merge to left and store the full merged table in merged. Select only students whose Quiz is missing into result, keeping Student_ID, Name, and Quiz, then print result. Filling an unmatched assessment with zero changes its meaning; agree on a policy first.

title: Audit both unmatched sides
text:
Merge related tables An outer merge keeps keys from either table. indicator=True adds a _merge column showing left_only, right_only, or both. This is a simple way to find records that need review. audit = students().merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="outer", indicator=True, validate="one_to_one")
result = audit.loc[audit["_merge"].ne("both"), ["Student_ID", "_merge"]]
print(result)
print("All merged rows:", len(audit)) Use a right merge instead. Keep indicator=True and report the row that has no registered student name. Pandas may match missing keys to other missing keys; audit or reject null keys before important merges.

title: Stop duplicate-key expansion
text:
Merge related tables If a lookup repeats a key, one input row can produce several output rows. The code deliberately adds a duplicate AI lookup. Catching MergeError lets us demonstrate the problem without stopping the lesson. bad_lookup = pd.concat([departments(), departments().iloc[[0]]], ignore_index=True)
blocked = False
try:
    students().merge(bad_lookup, on="Program", validate="many_to_one")
except pd.errors.MergeError:
    blocked = True
    print("Blocked: Program is not unique in the lookup.")
result = students().merge(bad_lookup, on="Program")
print("Rows without validation:", len(result)) Remove only exact duplicate lookup rows, confirm Program is unique, and perform the validated merge. validate checks the relationship; it does not decide how to repair conflicting records.

title: Stack row batches
text:
Concatenate and align concat stacks tables when axis=0, the default. ignore_index=True assigns new position labels. This changes the index, not the Student_ID values. df = students()
first = df.iloc[:6]
second = df.iloc[6:]
result = pd.concat([first, second], ignore_index=True)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name"]]) Stack the second batch before the first, and reset the index in the combined result. Build a list of batches and concatenate once instead of repeatedly growing a DataFrame in a loop.

title: Align columns by labels
text:
Concatenate and align concat with axis=1 places objects side by side. It matches index labels, even when their order differs. This is why an ID index is safer than assuming row positions match. names = pd.Series(["Amira", "Bilal"], index=["S001", "S002"], name="Name")
scores = pd.Series([72, 88], index=["S002", "S001"], name="Score")
result = pd.concat([names, scores], axis=1)
print(result) Add score 91 for S003, then concatenate using join="inner" so only shared IDs remain. Resetting indexes before concatenating unrelated tables can hide a mismatched-key problem.

title: Request a specific index order
text:
Concatenate and align reindex requests specific labels in a specific order. A requested label that does not exist produces missing values. It can also omit existing labels that were not requested. df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
result = df.reindex(["S003", "S001", "S099"])[["Name", "Score"]]
print(result) Reindex to S012, S002, S001 and print the Name and Score columns in that order. Reindexing generally requires unique labels on the axis being reindexed.

title: Fill from a second source
text:
Concatenate and align combine_first fills missing values from matching labels in another object. Existing non-missing values in the first source win. Agree which source has priority before applying this rule. primary = pd.Series([88, pd.NA, 91], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], dtype="Int64")
backup = pd.Series([85, 72, 90], index=["S001", "S002", "S003"], dtype="Int64")
result = primary.combine_first(backup)
print(result) Reverse the source priority by calling combine_first on backup. Explain the S001 result. An unmatched backup label can expand the index; inspect the result size.

title: Melt wide columns into rows
text:
Reshape tables A wide table stores different measures in different columns. melt turns selected measure columns into a label column and a value column. The ID is repeated so every new row still belongs to a student. wide = students().head(3)[["Student_ID", "Score", "Attendance"]]
result = wide.melt(id_vars="Student_ID", value_vars=["Score", "Attendance"], var_name="Measure", value_name="Value")
print(result) Use the first four students and melt Score and Study_Hours instead. A shared Value column may contain measures with different units; keep and use Measure.

title: Pivot a unique pair
text:
Reshape tables pivot moves distinct category labels into columns. Every index-and-column pair must identify at most one value. Here each student has one Score and one Attendance value. long = students().head(3).melt(id_vars="Student_ID", value_vars=["Score", "Attendance"], var_name="Measure", value_name="Value")
result = long.pivot(index="Student_ID", columns="Measure", values="Value")
print(result) Pivot the same long table so Measure labels form the rows and Student_ID labels form the columns. Use pivot_table only when you actually intend to aggregate repeated pairs.

title: Aggregate with pivot_table
text:
Reshape tables Several students share the same Campus and Program. pivot_table can reduce those repeated combinations using an explicit aggregation function. Naming aggfunc makes the summary rule clear. df = students()
result = df.pivot_table(index="Campus", columns="Program", values="Score", aggfunc="mean", observed=True)
print(result.round(2)) Change the table to count Student_ID records for each campus and program. Filling an absent combination with zero implies a meaning; it is not automatically appropriate for a mean.

title: Count combinations with crosstab
text:
Reshape tables crosstab counts how often two categories occur together. normalize="index" instead reports proportions within each row. The denominator changes, so always label the result. df = students()
result = pd.crosstab(df["Campus"], df["Program"])
print(result) Calculate program percentages within each campus and keep the unrounded percentages in result. Print a version rounded to one decimal place. Say whether percentages are by row, by column, or of the whole table.

title: Read and export CSV
text:
Read and write files CSV stores text rows separated by delimiters. read_csv creates a DataFrame and attempts to infer column types. to_csv writes the selected data; index=False avoids saving the pandas row index as an extra column. df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", dtype={"Student_ID": "string"})
result = df.loc[df["Score"].ge(85), ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
result.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "high_scores.csv", index=False)
print(result)
print("Saved outputs/high_scores.csv") Read only Student_ID, Name, and Attendance. Save students with Attendance below 85 to attendance_followup.csv. CSV does not preserve every pandas dtype. Check types and missing-value rules when reloading.

title: Move records through JSON
text:
Read and write files JSON can store a list of records, each represented by a dictionary. orient="records" makes this structure explicit. Re-reading a file checks that the exported shape matches what you intended. df = pd.read_json(DATA_DIR / "students.json", orient="records")
result = df[["Student_ID", "Campus", "Score"]].head(3)
result.to_json(OUTPUT_DIR / "student_preview.json", orient="records", indent=2)
print(result)
print((OUTPUT_DIR / "student_preview.json").read_text()) Export Student_ID and Program for the first two students, then read the saved JSON back into result. File formats can change date and nullable dtype representations; a round trip needs validation.

title: Select an Excel worksheet
text:
Read and write files An Excel workbook can contain several sheets. sheet_name selects one by name. The openpyxl engine handles the provided .xlsx workbook and is listed in the installation requirements. df = pd.read_excel(DATA_DIR / "students.xlsx", sheet_name="Students", engine="openpyxl")
result = df.groupby("Campus", as_index=False)["Score"].mean()
result.to_excel(OUTPUT_DIR / "campus_report.xlsx", sheet_name="Summary", index=False, engine="openpyxl")
print(result.round(2)) Read the Students sheet. Store a summary in result with columns Program and Students, where Students counts rows per program. Export it to program_counts.xlsx, sheet Counts. If openpyxl is missing, install the provided requirements before running this cell.

title: Query a small SQLite table
text:
Read and write files SQL retrieves data from tables using a query. This example creates a temporary in-memory database from the fictional data. The parameter placeholder passes a value separately from the query text. with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    students().to_sql("students", connection, index=False, if_exists="replace")
    result = pd.read_sql_query(
        "SELECT Student_ID, Name, Score FROM students WHERE Score >= ? ORDER BY Score DESC",
        connection, params=(85,))
print(result) Use SQL to calculate mean Score and student count for each Campus. Store the returned DataFrame in result with columns Campus, Mean_Score, and Students, ordered by Campus. Only use if_exists="replace" here on the temporary classroom table; on a real database it replaces the existing table.

title: Expose a missing day
text:
Work with time series A DatetimeIndex lets pandas work with calendar dates. asfreq("D") requests a daily index between the first and last observations. The missing October 4 row appears as unknown, not zero. df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
print(result) Build the daily Series and select only entries whose visitor count is missing. Store that filtered Series, retaining its date index, in result and print it. asfreq does not aggregate. Ensure the date index is unique before requesting a frequency.

title: Resample into calendar bins
text:
Work with time series resample groups observations into time bins. Here each bin starts at a three-day boundary measured from the first day. Report the number of observations beside the total so a partial bin is visible. df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
s = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index()
groups = s.resample("3D")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Recorded_Total": groups.sum(min_count=1), "Observed_Days": groups.count()})
print(result) Resample to individual days and use sum(min_count=1) so October 4 stays missing. Store only the daily total Series, indexed by date, in result. Time-bin labels and boundaries depend on frequency and options; state the reporting period.

title: Calculate a rolling mean
text:
Work with time series A rolling window calculates a statistic repeatedly as it moves through the data. On this daily grid, rolling(3) means three calendar rows. min_periods=3 requires three known counts, so windows crossing the missing day stay unknown. df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Visitors": daily, "Mean_3_Days": daily.rolling(3, min_periods=3).mean()})
print(result.round(2)) Calculate a two-day rolling mean requiring two known daily counts. Store only the resulting mean Series, indexed by date, in result. Sort time data before rolling. Otherwise the window follows an unintended order.

title: Compare with a previous period
text:
Work with time series shift(1) places the previous row value beside the current row. pct_change(fill_method=None) calculates fractional change without filling gaps. Multiplying by 100 expresses that change as a percentage. df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Visitors": daily, "Previous_Day": daily.shift(1), "Change_Percent": daily.pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100})
print(result.round(2)) Calculate the signed difference in visitor counts from two calendar days earlier using shift(2). Store the difference Series, indexed by date, in result. Percent change from a previous zero is undefined; inspect zero denominators.

title: Create a MultiIndex
text:
Explore richer structures A MultiIndex stores more than one label per row. Here Campus and Student_ID jointly locate a student. sort_index arranges the levels for predictable selection. df = students().set_index(["Campus", "Student_ID"]).sort_index()
result = df.loc[("RAK", "S003"), ["Name", "Score"]]
print(result) Use xs to select all Dubai students at the Campus level and print Name and Score. A tuple used as a MultiIndex key is different from a list of separate row keys.

title: Stack and unstack
text:
Explore richer structures stack moves column labels into an additional row-index level. unstack moves an index level back into columns. The explicit future_stack=True selects the modern stack implementation on pandas 2.2 and 3.x. wide = students().head(2).set_index("Student_ID")[["Score", "Attendance"]]
result = wide.stack(future_stack=True)
print(result) Stack the first three students and unstack the last level back into a DataFrame. Check that it equals the original wide table. Missing combinations can appear when reshaping sparse data; inspect the resulting shape.

title: Expand lists with explode
text:
Explore richer structures Sometimes one cell contains several items, such as a list of skills. explode creates a separate row for each item and repeats the other columns. This changes the unit of analysis from one row per student to one row per student-skill. df = pd.DataFrame({"Student_ID": ["S001", "S002"], "Skills": [["Python", "SQL"], ["Excel"]]})
result = df.explode("Skills", ignore_index=True)
print(result) Give S002 a second skill, SQL. Explode the table, then store the count of student-skill rows for each skill in result as a value_counts() Series. An empty list becomes a row with a missing item; a string that looks like a list is still a string.

title: Order and encode categories
text:
Explore richer structures Categorical values can follow a chosen order instead of alphabetical order. get_dummies makes one indicator column per category. These indicator values describe membership, not a numerical ranking. df = students().head(4).copy()
df["Program"] = pd.Categorical(df["Program"], categories=["IT", "AI"], ordered=True)
ordered = df.sort_values("Program", kind="stable")
result = pd.get_dummies(ordered["Program"], prefix="Program", dtype=int)
print(ordered[["Student_ID", "Program"]])
print(result) Change the category order to AI then IT and print the sorted student IDs and dummy columns. Values outside a specified category list become missing; validate allowed categories first.

title: Measure memory use
text:
Work efficiently and reproducibly memory_usage(deep=True) estimates memory including text stored by object columns. Repeated labels may use less memory as categories. The benefit depends on the data, so measure it instead of assuming. labels = pd.Series(["RAK", "Dubai"] * 500, dtype=object)
category = labels.astype("category")
result = pd.Series({"Object_bytes": labels.memory_usage(deep=True), "Category_bytes": category.memory_usage(deep=True)})
print(result) Measure 1,000 unique text labels before and after category conversion. Explain why the saving may shrink or disappear. This is a small storage demonstration, not a benchmark of all pandas workloads.

title: Load only needed columns
text:
Work efficiently and reproducibly usecols avoids reading columns that the question does not need. Explicit dtypes make the import contract clearer. This small file demonstrates a habit that becomes useful with larger files. result = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Student_ID", "Program", "Score"], dtype={"Student_ID": "string", "Program": "category"})
print(result.head())
print(result.dtypes) Read only Student_ID and Attendance, and limit the preview to the first four file rows with nrows. A file preview can miss problems that occur later in the file.

title: Combine chunk totals correctly
text:
Work efficiently and reproducibly chunksize reads a CSV in pieces. A total and a non-missing count can be accumulated across pieces without keeping all rows. Divide the overall total by the overall count to calculate the overall mean. total = 0
count = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Score"], chunksize=5):
    total += chunk["Score"].sum()
    count += chunk["Score"].count()
result = total / count
print("Known scores:", count)
print("Mean score:", round(result, 2)) Use chunks of four rows and calculate how many students score at least 80 without retaining all rows. Not every operation is easy to compute in chunks. A global sort or median needs a different strategy.

title: Take a repeatable sample
text:
Work efficiently and reproducibly sample chooses rows randomly. random_state makes the selection repeatable for this data and environment. Reproducibility does not make a tiny sample representative of the population. df = students()
result = df.sample(n=3, random_state=7)
repeat = df.sample(n=3, random_state=7)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Campus", "Score"]])
print("Same sample:", result.equals(repeat)) Take two students from each campus using groupby.sample with random_state=7. Document input data, row order, library versions, and seed when an exact sample matters.

title: Compare groups with bars
text:
Plot and interpret A bar chart compares categories. First calculate one statistic per group, then plot those values. The axis label must say whether the height is a mean, count, or total. df = students()
result = df.groupby("Campus")["Score"].mean().sort_index()
ax = result.plot.bar(color="#28756a", rot=0, figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Mean score by campus (practice data)", xlabel="Campus", ylabel="Mean score (out of 100)", ylim=(0, 100))
plt.tight_layout()
print(result.round(2))
plt.show() Plot the number of students in each Program instead, with a count label on the y-axis. Use a zero baseline for ordinary bar comparisons so bar length remains meaningful.

title: Inspect a distribution
text:
Plot and interpret A histogram counts numeric observations within intervals called bins. It shows the distribution of individual values, rather than a summary for each named category. Bin choices can change the visual impression. df = students()
result = pd.cut(df["Score"], bins=[50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100], right=False).value_counts(sort=False)
ax = df["Score"].plot.hist(bins=[50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100], color="#28756a", edgecolor="white", figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Distribution of scores (practice data)", xlabel="Score (out of 100)", ylabel="Number of students")
plt.tight_layout()
print(result)
plt.show() Use wider bins [50, 75, 100] and compare the count table and visual shape. Histogram libraries usually include the upper endpoint of the last bin; pd.cut(right=False) does not. These sample scores contain no endpoint value of 100.

title: Compare two measurements
text:
Plot and interpret A scatter plot places one point at each pair of numeric measurements. This can reveal a pattern, an unusual observation, or a gap. Correlation describes association; it does not establish why the pattern occurs. df = students()
result = df[["Study_Hours", "Score"]].corr().loc["Study_Hours", "Score"]
ax = df.plot.scatter(x="Study_Hours", y="Score", color="#28756a", figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.set(title="Study time and score (practice data)", xlabel="Study hours per week", ylabel="Score (out of 100)")
plt.tight_layout()
print("Pearson correlation:", round(result, 3))
plt.show() Plot Attendance against Score and calculate their Pearson correlation. Outliers, restricted ranges, and missing data can affect correlation; inspect the actual points.

title: Show change over time
text:
Plot and interpret A line chart uses an ordered horizontal axis to show change. Reindexing to a daily grid keeps the missing date visible as a gap. A line across an unobserved day can otherwise suggest continuity that was not measured. df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
ax.plot(result.index, result, marker="o", color="#28756a")
ax.set(title="Daily visitors (practice data)", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Recorded visitors")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.tight_layout()
print(result)
plt.show() Store the daily counts in daily and the three-day rolling mean in result, requiring three known daily values. Plot daily and result together with labels for both lines. A smooth line does not create new observations; report how any smoothing was calculated.

title: A label is not a row position
text:
Debugging clinic A table can use student IDs as its index. Position 0 still means the first row, but the label of that row is now S001. Read the index before choosing a selector. df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
by_position = df.iloc[0:2][["Name", "Score"]]
by_label = df.loc["S001":"S002", ["Name", "Score"]]
print(by_position)
print("Same rows:", by_position.equals(by_label)) Select S003 through S005 by label, then select the same three students by position. Print both and confirm equality. An integer inside loc is a label, even when it looks like a row number.

title: Repair a condition with two rules
text:
Debugging clinic A filter must produce one True or False value per row. Combine pandas conditions with & for AND or | for OR, with parentheses around each comparison. The broken expression is a comment so this example can run. df = students()
# Broken: df[(df["Score"] >= 80) and (df["Attendance"] >= 90)]
mask = (df["Score"] >= 80) & (df["Attendance"] >= 90)
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Score", "Attendance"]]
print(result) Find students whose Score is below 70 OR whose Attendance is below 80. Print their IDs and both values. Do not remove the parentheses around each comparison.

title: Change the table you actually intend to change
text:
Debugging clinic A filtered table and the original table are different objects. Use a single .loc assignment when the original must change. Use .copy() when creating a separate working table, and inspect both afterward. df = students()
mask = df["Student_ID"].eq("S004")
# Avoid: df[mask]["Score"] = 70
df.loc[mask, "Score"] = 70
result = df.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Score"]]
print(result) Start with a fresh df = students() and create a separate copy of its RAK rows named rak. Add 5 points to scores in rak. Show that Amira's copied score is 93 while her score in df remains 88. A method returning a new object is not an instruction to update the old one.

title: A correct total can still hide a bad merge
text:
Debugging clinic Two tables may contain the same key more than once. Matching repeated keys can multiply records. Validate the intended relationship and inspect unmatched IDs before calculating a report. left = students()[["Student_ID", "Name"]]
right = assessment()
result = left.merge(right, on="Student_ID", how="outer",
                    validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
print(result.loc[result["_merge"].ne("both"), ["Student_ID", "_merge"]])
print("Rows:", len(result)) Keep only enrolled students with a left merge stored in result. Keep the merge indicator column, and store the count of students with no assessment in missing_count. Do not remove duplicate keys without understanding why they exist.

title: Clean the raw table and keep an audit trail
text:
End-to-end classroom project Bring the cleaning skills together. Remove the known exact duplicate, normalize labels, preserve why a score is unavailable, and flag impossible attendance as missing. This exercise makes no assumption that an absent score equals zero. df = raw_students().drop_duplicates().copy()
df["Name"] = df["Name"].astype("string").str.strip()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].astype("string").str.strip().str.title()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].replace({"Rak": "RAK"})
df["Score_Status"] = "recorded"
df.loc[df["Score"].isna(), "Score_Status"] = "missing"
df.loc[df["Score"].eq("absent"), "Score_Status"] = "absent"
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Study_Hours"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Study_Hours"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].astype("Float64")
df.loc[~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100), "Attendance"] = pd.NA
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

print(df[["Student_ID", "Name", "Campus", "Score", "Score_Status", "Attendance"]])
print("Rows:", len(df))
print("Unavailable scores:", df["Score"].isna().sum()) Use the cleaned table to create a review list containing students with a missing Score, Study_Hours, or Attendance. Store it in result with columns Student_ID, Score, Study_Hours, and Attendance, then print result. Do not discard the raw labels before you have recorded their meaning.

title: Report a mean with its denominator
text:
End-to-end classroom project A group average is easier to interpret when its sample count is visible. Count all students and count recorded scores separately. Pandas mean skips missing numeric scores by default; say that in your report. df = raw_students().drop_duplicates().copy()
df["Name"] = df["Name"].astype("string").str.strip()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].astype("string").str.strip().str.title()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].replace({"Rak": "RAK"})
df["Score_Status"] = "recorded"
df.loc[df["Score"].isna(), "Score_Status"] = "missing"
df.loc[df["Score"].eq("absent"), "Score_Status"] = "absent"
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Study_Hours"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Study_Hours"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].astype("Float64")
df.loc[~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100), "Attendance"] = pd.NA
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

result = (df.groupby("Campus", as_index=False)
          .agg(Students=("Student_ID", "size"),
               Recorded_Scores=("Score", "count"),
               Mean_Score=("Score", "mean")))
print(result.round(2)) Produce the same report by Program. Add Missing_Scores = Students - Recorded_Scores, then sort from highest to lowest Mean_Score. A polished mean without the number of observed values can mislead.

title: Join, audit, and select a follow-up list
text:
End-to-end classroom project Combine the cleaned records with assessment results, checking both match quality and row counts. The follow-up rule below uses an observed Score under 75 or a missing assessment. Unknown scores need separate review, not automatic failure. df = raw_students().drop_duplicates().copy()
df["Name"] = df["Name"].astype("string").str.strip()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].astype("string").str.strip().str.title()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].replace({"Rak": "RAK"})
df["Score_Status"] = "recorded"
df.loc[df["Score"].isna(), "Score_Status"] = "missing"
df.loc[df["Score"].eq("absent"), "Score_Status"] = "absent"
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Study_Hours"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Study_Hours"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].astype("Float64")
df.loc[~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100), "Attendance"] = pd.NA
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

joined = df.merge(assessment(), on="Student_ID", how="left",
                  validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
mask = joined["Score"].lt(75).fillna(False) | joined["_merge"].eq("left_only")
result = joined.loc[mask, ["Student_ID", "Score", "Quiz", "_merge"]]
print(result) Create a separate audit with an outer merge. Show only unmatched IDs and whether each ID belongs to the student table or the assessment table. A missing comparison may propagate pd.NA; decide how the rule treats unknowns.

title: Create a table, a plot, and a reproducible export
text:
End-to-end classroom project Finish with a compact report and a plot that answers a stated question. Keep the clean table and the summary as separate outputs. On a new run, rebuild the report from the source and the written cleaning rules. df = raw_students().drop_duplicates().copy()
df["Name"] = df["Name"].astype("string").str.strip()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].astype("string").str.strip().str.title()
df["Campus"] = df["Campus"].replace({"Rak": "RAK"})
df["Score_Status"] = "recorded"
df.loc[df["Score"].isna(), "Score_Status"] = "missing"
df.loc[df["Score"].eq("absent"), "Score_Status"] = "absent"
df["Score"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Score"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Study_Hours"] = pd.to_numeric(df["Study_Hours"], errors="coerce").astype("Float64")
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].astype("Float64")
df.loc[~df["Attendance"].between(0, 100), "Attendance"] = pd.NA
df["Join_Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Join_Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")

result = df.pivot_table(index="Campus", columns="Program", values="Score",
                        aggfunc="mean", observed=True)
counts = df.pivot_table(index="Campus", columns="Program", values="Score",
                        aggfunc="count", observed=True)
print("Recorded mean scores:")
print(result.round(2))
print("Recorded score counts:")
print(counts)
ax = result.plot.bar(color=["#216b62", "#b58b45"], rot=0)
ax.set_title("Recorded mean score by campus and program")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean score (0–100)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
df.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "capstone_cleaned_students.csv", index=False)
result.round(2).to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "capstone_score_summary.csv")
counts.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "capstone_recorded_counts.csv")
print("Saved cleaned data, summary, and recorded counts in outputs/.") Make a Program-level report with columns Program, Recorded_Scores, and Mean_Score. Export it without a DataFrame index to capstone_program_report.csv. Read the exported file back into read_back and verify its columns and row count. CSV does not preserve every pandas dtype. Recheck dtypes when loading it later.

text:
Import CSV and text with confidence The bundled Palmer Penguins CSV is a real public dataset, preserved from its authoritative upstream source. Read the field definitions in data/public/README.md before interpreting its values. The simplified table records 344 observations, eight fields, and source missing values written as NA. path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(path, na_values=["NA"])
result = df.head(5)
print(result)
print("Shape:", df.shape)
print("Columns:", df.columns.tolist())
print("Missing values:")
print(df.isna().sum()) Read only species, island, and body_mass_g using usecols. Store the full three-column table in result and print its shape and the number of known body masses. These are historical study observations from 2007–2009, not current measurements or a population census.

Import CSV and text with confidence A text file does not need a .csv extension to hold a table. Its delimiter determines where fields begin and end. The TSV and TXT files here are documented format conversions of the same public observations, so you can compare the imports directly. path = DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.tsv"
wrong = pd.read_csv(path, sep=",")
result = pd.read_csv(path, sep="\t", na_values=["NA"])

print("With a tab separator:", result.shape)
